subject: TrueCap #12 — seller financing, when it actually wins
preheader: When to ask · How to structure · Why most investors avoid it (and shouldn't) · 3 deals

marketSnapshot.headline: Bond market pricing in a September cut
marketSnapshot.body: 10-year Treasury dropped 18bp this week on softer CPI, and the 30Y mortgage followed — currently 6.51%. Fed funds futures now price 85% odds of a September cut, with 60% probability of a 50bp cut (not just 25). If that happens, expect another 25-40bp leg lower on mortgage rates through October. For investors negotiating offers in August, this is great timing — you can underwrite at today's rates and likely refi in 12-18 months at meaningfully better terms.

dealSpotter.address: Kansas City, MO — Brookside SFR (seller financing)
dealSpotter.body: $245k 3/2 at $1,975 rent. Seller is a retired owner who's been managing the property for 18 years and wants out, but doesn't want the tax hit of an outright sale this year. Structured: $12,250 down (5%), $232,750 seller-financed at 6.0%, 7-year balloon. Compared to a conventional 25% down at 6.8%: you keep $48,750 of capital that's deploying elsewhere, and you save 80bp on rate. The balloon is the only risk — you need a refinance path in year 6-7. Plan for it from day one.

$485k 2-unit. Original ask was full conventional. After 75 days on market, the seller's agent floated 'we'd entertain seller-carry' to break the stalemate. Negotiated 10% down with seller carrying 15% second, conventional first for the rest. The second is interest-only for 5 years. Net effect: cap rate on cash invested jumps from 7.1% to 7.7% because the principal payments on the second are paused for 5 years.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Owner offered 100% financing · too good to be true · WALK
dealSpotter.body: $72k 3/1 listed. Seller (a wholesaler holding it as a rental) offered 100% seller financing at 7.5%. The math looks amazing — zero capital deployed, immediate positive cash flow. The catch: the property has a Section 8 tenant with two missed payments and a pending eviction filing. The seller is using 100% financing to offload a problem property onto someone who'll do less due diligence. Always ask 'why does this seller want this structure?' If you can't get a clear answer, walk.

blogFeature.title: Cap rate vs cash-on-cash vs DSCR — which metric actually matters?
blogFeature.excerpt: Three different metrics, three different questions they answer. Why most investors quote cap rate when they should be looking at cash-on-cash, and why your lender cares only about DSCR.

qa.question: When does it make sense to ASK a seller for financing vs go conventional?
qa.answer: Four scenarios where asking is reasonable. (1) The property has been on market 60+ days — the seller is feeling the carrying cost and is open to creative solutions. (2) The seller is a long-time owner (5+ years) with significant equity and known tax exposure — seller financing spreads their capital gains across multiple years. (3) You have strong negotiating cards (cash buyer, fast close, no inspection contingency) you can trade for favorable terms. (4) You'd otherwise not be able to qualify or want to preserve conventional credit slots for other deals. The wrong scenarios: when the seller has a mortgage they need to pay off at sale (most do — they can't seller-finance), when the property is brand-new on market (the seller hasn't felt pain yet), or when the structure introduces a balloon you don't have a credible refinance plan for.
